utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please stand and read aloud the affirmation on the card?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I thank the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness P-021, my name is Moore. I prosecute in this case. I think you have seen Ms. Tuma we look a little different as others know. You have been recalled to deal with three documents which the Prosecution served on the Defence after you had concluded your evidence. I will tender this witness, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. My name is Miroslav Vasic, in case you don't remember from our last encounter. I would like to ask you to pause after hearing my question so that everything we say can be interpreted and so that your voice does not leak through my microphone. Please tell me: On the 9th of June, 1994, did you speak with the officials of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia about the events which took place in Vukovar Hospital in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that on that occasion you spoke to a gentleman called Miroslav Filipcic who drafted an official note following his interview with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that a certain gentleman talked to me. I'm not sure about the name, but yes, I did talk to a man.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 22nd of February, 1996, did you also testify before the investigative judge of the county court in Zagreb in a case against the accused Veljko Kadijevic and others, and did you sign the statement you gave to the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I did speak to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you spoke to the officials of the Ministry of the Interior, you covered the events from November of 1991 as well as some documents which were drafted by you in November of 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we go to look at these documents, let me ask you this: In that period of time, 1994, 1996, 1997, did you also speak with the officials of the security and information agency of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean that you don't remember having a conversation with them, or you did not speak to them at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, no, I did not speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you speak about the Vukovar events with some of the officials of the security and information agency of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the document, the document that you mentioned just a little bit ago, then yes. But nothing outside of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will now turn to this document. I think that it could potentially disclose the identity of this witness, so perhaps we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Would you please play this tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I believe that we have a sound problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would my learned friend have any translation to help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, unfortunately I must say that the -- right now I do not have -- I do not have a translation. The interpreters will follow the text on the screen and interpret it for you, and I will submit you an official translation the minute I have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's assuming we get some sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Sinisa Glavasevic is reading this indictment for Radio 101. We cannot claim with certainty that it was ever published in the Croatian media. This is an indictment whereby I charge the Assembly of the Republic of Croatia for the participation of Croats in the greatest crime in history over the Croatian people for taking part in the decision to sacrifice tens of thousands of lives of Croats from Vukovar. I accuse you, gentlemen, for having allowed for them to go hungry while you were sated, because you were warm and they were cold, while you were actually assuaging your thirst with drinks according to your own choice and in desired quantities. You just left them to a cupful of water, to a spoonful of water a day. Assemblymen, you spent your days in your luxurious homes and your impressive offices, and you gave the Vukovar people muddy and dark dungeons, cellars. For your nights you chose warm and soft blankets, and to them you left dirty and squalid quarters and blankets. Do you really think that this is what these people voted for? Why did you condemn our children and our babies to smallpox -- to infection, rather. Are all the infections of the world reserved for the children of Vukovar? I accuse you, assemblymen, for all their pain, for all the dust filling the children's eyes, for every stifled shout, cry, for all the shed tears and all that were unshed. I accuse you, assemblymen, for every heroic hand, arm, which was cut from living flesh, for every wound that was dressed without anaesthetic, and for every surgery taken in this way. I accuse you for all the pains of the hungry and thirsty, wounded, for all the desperation and fatigue of our physicians and other medical staff. I accuse you for all the deaths which resulted because of the lack of blood plasma and adequate medicines. I accuse you for all the desperation of the fighter when he realised that he has nothing to use to fill his -- to use as ammunition for his weapons. I accuse you, assemblymen, for the moment of surprise when it -- the -- when material evidence, irrefutable material evidence reached Vukovar to the effect that the Republic of Croatia have the personnel and all the resources necessary to break through the road and for the defence of Vukovar but does not want to use the same, i.e., to submit the same to the command of the operation group of Vukovar, Vinkovci, Zupanja, which command requested -- which the command requested in order to carry out the tasks set before them. I accuse you, gentlemen, for all the pain of the moment in which Vukovar realised that between you, the Croatian Assembly, the Croatian government, the president of the Republic of Croatia and the Chetniks was no difference at all. I accuse you, gentlemen, for all the disgrace that you inflicted on the Croatian people representing it. The Croatian people did not authorise you for this, and therefore I accuse you of treason. I accuse you, gentlemen, because you stood in front of the sanctuary of the Croatian people, what is sacrosanct to the Croatian people and the Croatian tri-colour, and traitors can never allow themselves to do that. You have besmirched our flag and that is why I am accusing you. I am accusing you for having sung with your criminal mouths our beautiful anthem which used to be sung by the heroes of the Trpinja road, the heros of Luzac, the heros of Mitnica, of Sajmiste, Borovo Naselje, the heroes of Bogdanovci. The heroes of Vukovar sang it as they were defending Vukovar in the thick of fighting, when they were burying the dismembered remains of their friends. They sang it as they were dying. I accuse you, gentlemen, for having arrogated that right unto yourselves as well. It is inadmissible for you under whose blessing Vukovar is dying to sing the song of the people whom you have condemned to a martyr's death. I accuse you for having participated in a massacre, in a massacre of the population and defenders of Vukovar. I accuse you, gentlemen, for the death of Vukovar. The material proof of your indubitable guilt will be given to the Croatian people to see and to the entire world public. Do not delude yourself that you will come before them. You cannot. We are shelling. We are -- we are -- guarantee, sorry. We also guarantee that in the future you shall enter the annals of history as traitors and criminals and that until the end of your lives you will go to bed and wake up with a memory of Vukovar. Signed Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you whether you recognised the voice of Sinisa Glavasevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. Although the recording was quite bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see the address he gave on the Radio 101 on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, before you pass on, the Chamber would like to record its appreciation of the interpreter who had a great difficulty with the speed of that rather lengthy written passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would also like to join in your remark. This was quite a task for the interpreters. I would like to tender this audio recording into evidence. We will provide the official transcription of this audio recording in English as soon as we receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have no objection to it being tendered for the truth of its content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 351.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you kindly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me: Did the doctors know whether some patients left the hospital, came back, were they able to follow the whereabouts of each patient at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: It was impossible to know at all times where somebody is. One can only be responsible for oneself. Sometimes I was unable to say where my own nurse was, the nurse that always worked with me. One can only claim with certainty about oneself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you. Similarly, one cannot really say where the patients were, and what they did, unless they were under constant care of their doctors. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: One can say with certainty where a person is if one is with that person. And as for everything else, I apologise, a hospital is not a prison, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Certainly, and fortunately that it isn't. Thank you for your answers. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. I would like to ask the usher to give me back the copies of official notes. We will submit a copy of these documents to the registrar so that they can be filed electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do we understand you do not tender them?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I covered the most important details the witness confirmed that and explained, I don't see any reason to tender this into evidence. I think that transcript alone is clear. At least in relation to what is important for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The document will be marked for identification, not as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will be marked for identification with number 352.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honours, I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not a misfortune, Mr. Borovic, for either of us. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this will be joyous news for you, I have only one question for this witness. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... document in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. My name is Novak Lukic. I represent Mr. Sljivancanin. Let me remind what you stated in answer to the questions of the Prosecutor on the 9th of November, 2005, relating to the meeting you had in the plaster room with Mr. Sljivancanin. On page 1371 of the transcript, you said that the meeting lasted half an hour to 45 minutes. And then you stated as follows: [In English] And during that time he spoke to us in general about the political situation, about the break-up of Yugoslavia, how that came about. He told us that he understood us as a medical staff. He realised that we just did our job and that it was the natural that we did so. And that he wouldn't take that against us. It was along these lines. [Interpretation] That's how you described what you remembered about Sljivancanin telling you on that occasion. You later said in cross-examination that you did not remember a lot of details because you had a lot of your own thoughts to deal with. Now, this official note, which is a record of the conversation that you had on the 9th of June, 1994, this record is in the third person singular. I will now read to you page 2, paragraph 3, as to how you described this back in 1994. I would like to see whether this would refresh your memory. I'm interested in only one sentence you uttered on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: I apologise, would you be so kind and translate for me what you read out from the transcript? You read it out in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that you were receiving interpretation. You weren't. All right. Let me go over it again. "During that meeting, which lasted about half an hour to 45 minutes, Sljivancanin talked to in general about the political situation, about the break-up of Yugoslavia, and how that came about. He told you that he understood medical personnel, he understood that all you did was do your job and that he wasn't going to take that against you." Roughly this is what your recollections were. I will now read this passage, and you can follow to make sure that I'm reading it out correctly, this portion of the official note from 1994. "On the 20th of November, 1991, early in the morning the head nurse Binazija Kolesar" -- her name is recorded wrongly here, it should be Kolesar -- "came into the room and told them to get ready and that they were to come to the main surgical room for a meeting. When they arrived there, they saw a former JNA officer who introduced himself as Sljivancanin. He told them that he was a JNA officer, and that their army had come to liberate them. He also said that they, hospital staff -- he also said that they did not consider the hospital staff as war criminals, because they, as medical staff, were duty-bound to help all the wounded. He suggested that they should continue working in the Vukovar Medical Centre, as there were many wounded, so that the hospital could be made operational as soon as possible. He said that people who did not wish to remain working in the hospital could say so openly and that they should also indicate where they would like to be evacuated to and that a list should be drawn reflecting who wished to go where." So my question is a very simple one. Do you remember that you gave this description to the police inspector, and does it refresh your memory now that Mr. Sljivancanin, at the meeting, said that medical personnel could stay if they wished so, and those who wanted to leave should state whether they wanted to go to Croatia or to Serbia? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an account of our conversation, and I don't think that there are any discrepancies in relation to what I stated previously. I never claimed that medical personnel was denied the opportunity to state whether they wished to stay or leave. Yes, that opportunity was given to us, and I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention that while giving evidence, and that's why I wanted to clarify that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 0021 [sic], can I ask you questions arising out of the document that Mr. Lukic has been referring you to? He quoted a passage to you, and it ended with the words that: "They should also make a list who wanted to go where." Have you got that in front of you? Have you got the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just look at the next paragraph, please, so we have the totality of what occurred. Can I just read it out and see if it corresponds. "While he/Sljivancanin was saying that, (redacted) 0021 turned around and saw that the wounded people were being carried out through the corridor. As she recognised some of her wounded patients, she ran to them to talk to them, and asked them where they were being taken. But she was ordered to go back." Now, I am reading from the English translation. The phrase "while he/Sljivancanin was saying that," I would suggest tends to indicate that when you saw the patients being taken out Sljivancanin was present?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know if that is right or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. I think that I interrupted Mr. Moore, unfortunately. My objection is as follows: Everything that Mr. Moore just read out now was something that the witness told us in examination-in-chief. She told us all about this. The question that I put to her was unrelated to this. It was related to what Mr. Sljivancanin said at the meeting, and what Mr. Moore is now raising is -- was covered in examination-in-chief, which took place on the 9th of November, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question that was put by my learned friend was to convey an impression, in our submission, that Mr. Sljivancanin was a gentleman who was ensuring that people could go about their business as they wanted and was behaving in an honourable way. In our submission, if there is going to be that submission made, and it's a perfectly reasonable submission for my learned friend, then the totality of the behaviour at that time has to be placed before the Court so there is a general view of context, not just cherry-picking. And so I am merely submitting that if that is going to be submitted by my learned friend, and he opened the topic, then, quite simply, the totality of the evidence should be before the Court in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe the witness is not getting a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Lukic, your objection is overruled. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need interpretation because occasionally I am unable to grasp the entire context.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is obviously not on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we had a problem. The witness was not receiving interpretation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need interpretation into Croatian. I understand English, but these are complex matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand that. Are you now getting an interpretation of what I'm saying? I'm sorry about that. Hopefully you can now hear. And while that happened, I have redacted a name that was mentioned in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll repeat it, if I may. You were asked a question by Mr. Lukic, the gentleman with the beard, on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin. He asked you to -- or he read out a paragraph from the document that is being produced called the official note. You've got that in front of you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I deal then, please, you were asked about what Sljivancanin had said. I would like you please, to deal with the short paragraph. In English, it's only four lines. But I will read it out again and we'll see if you can follow it. "While he/Sljivancanin was saying that, turned around and saw that the wounded person" -- sorry, "the wounded people were being carried out through the corridor. As she recognised some of her wounded patients, she ran to them to talk to them and ask them where they were being taken, but she was ordered to go back." Now, this is what's called reported speech from the notes of June the 9th, 1994. The question that I have is this: It would appear from the way the paragraph is drafted, or written, and the use of the words "while he was saying that," that you saw something. Two questions: Firstly, who was it who ordered you to go back away from your patients?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: When I went out into the corridor, as I have told you here, I saw patients leaving, accompanied by soldiers. And the soldiers warned me that I needed to go back into the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal, then, please, with another topic? It's in relation to Mr. Vasic and the questions that he asked you about this same document. Now, can I ask you, please, to open that document in English it's 27804, but it deals with a list of people that are named by you during this interview. I'd like you, if you would be kind enough, to look at a document called MFI 345. Can I just indicate the reason why I'm going to ask you to do so, because you indicated you would need to see the hospital records of the level of injury of some of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'm going to try and do to shorten matters, I'm going to refer to the various numbers. So we have got number 2 is Vladimir Varga. Now, this is what is called a redacted list from the hospital that was collated in Zagreb. So the page that I'm going to ask you to look at is going to be the bottom right-hand corner. The page number. Can you see that? So if you look at the bottom right-hand corner, you will see a page number. If we deal with number 2, and we go to page 76, and we look halfway down the page - have you got that? - it seems to be the name of Varga, Vladimir. Is that the same Varga Vladimir that you have been referring to? Could you answer yes or no, please, for the record?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we go, then, to number 4, please? Number 4, can we go to page 38. Number 4, have you got that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is that the same name that is mentioned as number 4, the same person? We look right down at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we look then at number 5? Page 63. Again, if we look right at the bottom of the hospital record, is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Number 5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Number 6, page 61. Dmitar Pucar, middle of the page, is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 7, page 52. Towards the bottom of the page. Can you just confirm each time, because we do by way of microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Number 11, please. Page 21. Robert Gajda, three-fifths of the way down the page. Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Number 15. Should be page 24.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Number 18, page 29. Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Number 21, page 22.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This list of people that I think you have already told the Court on a previous occasion, they are the people who were wounded and on your ward; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to confirm that the people that you saw taken away that day by the JNA included some of these people on this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to approximate how many of these people that are named by myself were actually -- you actually saw taken away on the morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: From my list, two persons whose names I set aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who were those two that you actually saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: The wounded from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there may be a misunderstanding. You have told us about a list of people that were wounded and on your ward, and we have that list. You have told us about seeing patients being taken away on the morning of the 20th. And I think it's right to say that some of those patients that you saw taken away were your patients. What I'm trying to clarify is whether you were able to recognise any of the patients that were taken away on the 20th, whether they were any of the people on this list.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I'm asking you to estimate, if it's possible, whether it's all of them, some of them, approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think that it was already said. I'm sure about two persons, because I saw them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the name of the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether this should be in a private or in a public session, since we are mentioning the list from the ward, patients and so on. And even the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, but I -- I would I take it Mr. Moore knows or expects a certain answer and that it would not cause a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would hope not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is there any difficulty mentioning the names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names that you actually saw of the people taken away that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-021 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Grejza, Mr. Nikica Holjevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions in relation to this witness. I would ask that the document that my learned friend produced and cross-examined extensively on be made an exhibit. I think it's right to say that it actually links with the document that is already before the Court. I think it's Exhibit 62, but I just can't remember off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it was marked. Yes, I think that is correct. It was marked for identification. I would ask that it be made an exhibit. I have no objection to that. And I would equally submit that to some extent it marries up a document that is already before the Court, the core document, which is Exhibit 62, the handwritten list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, are we speaking of 345, the blue folder, or 352, the official note from 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document that I'm referring to is the official note from the 9th of June, 1994. I apologise if I'm wrong about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You gave just a lengthy explanation, I thought you were trying to justify the blue folder. I'm glad you're not, because you wouldn't have succeeded. But you will be allowed to tender Exhibit 352. And it's probably a good precaution that that be under seal, it's suggested by the court officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I have to problems for that. I think that is a wise precaution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, MFI 352 will become Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I thank you very much for coming again to The Hague and for the further assistance you have given us. I thank you for that and indicate that the questioning has now concluded. So, once again, you are free to return to your work and home. Thank you indeed. We will now have the first break. And because of a redaction, we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirm on the card that is given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Moore. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think he is enjoying a welcome day off, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, could you please state your full name, your age, and your current occupation, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm Slavoljub Kacarevic, I'm 49 years old, and I work in the marketing department of a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you are based in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When were you born, and where were you raised and schooled?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1956 in Belgrade and was schooled there and reared there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after schooling I believe that you trained as a journalist at the University of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you graduate from the university with the journalism degree?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Prior to that can you outline briefly your work experience, starting from your experience experiencing -- experience managing a private company in 1976. Can you explain what you did there, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: After I had enrolled in the university I pursued a private business for about three years, I had a small private company, until 1979. At that time I started to publish my work in a students' magazine on a regular basis, and since then have only been pursuing the journalistic profession until two years. So first I worked in the magazine student, then in the daily Politika, and then in Intervju, which was a magazine, and then in the daily called Glas Javnosti, the voice of the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can briefly run through your work career in journalism. In 1979 to 1980 you worked with the student magazine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, for about a year or so, a bit more than a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at that stage you were about 23 years of age?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is right. 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Court what your role was with that magazine, and what type of magazine it was, what audience it was aimed at?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: It was a state-owned paper, which was issued by the students' organisation of Belgrade, namely the Belgrade university, and it was intended primarily for students, but its readership also involved other segments of the public because it was interesting because of the free-thinking articles that were published in it, and could be published in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So the content of that magazine would have -- had political commentary?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- it would. Initially I worked as an associate, as a junior journalist, and later I was on the editorial team and I was one of the editors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Then you stated that you worked with the Politika newspaper. Was that between 1980 and 1989, approximately, for nine years?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the summer 1980 to the summer of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe the type of paper that that was, the audience it aimed at, and the subject content of that paper, back in those years?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: At that time Politika was the most prestigious daily in Serbia and probably in the then Yugoslavia. It was a general-type daily paper, which dealt with politics, but its content also contained all other topics interesting to a family. It had sports, cultural, and other topics, but politics was the dominant theme, and it was the most influential daily of its time in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was your job with that paper and what positions did you hold during those years?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: First I worked on the city column, and then the -- what was referred as the internal rubric or column, and occasionally I would stand in for the editor of the city column.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then in 1989 to 1995, did you work for Intervju magazine?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, from 1989 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was the subject -- the subject matter of that magazine, and what audience was it aimed at?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: It was a bi-weekly magazine, which carried interviews with personalities that the editors thought were in the limelight, were interesting enough, and deserved to be presented to the public, so the dominant content were such interviews. But apart from that, there were different articles and analyses, with the topics predominantly being of a political or historical character, but occasionally there would be some other articles; for instance, fashion or sports and the like. At that time it was a magazine that had the largest number of copies, one of the largest magazines with the largest circulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was your role with that magazine? What did you do and what positions did you hold during that period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning I was journalist, associate; later I was the deputy, or, rather, the assistant of the editor-in-chief; and later, after that, I worked as a journalist again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in 1991 were you working as a journalist in that position with the magazine?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Yes, I was, that year I was a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you left Intervju magazine in 1995, what was the next job you had, and for about how long did you have it before starting with the other newspaper, Glas Javnosti?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: After that I worked in a printing press for the printing of newspapers, and I was the director there for four years, until 1990. And then as of the beginning of -- 1999, and as of 1999 I worked as -- on the -- as the editor of the Glas Javnosti, and from 2004 I was the editor-in-chief of Glas Javnosti.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the name of the printing press company, was that ABC Graphic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe the newspaper Glas Javnosti, what type of paper it is -- is it, what type of subject matter?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: At that time when I worked on that paper, it was a daily of a general nature, which dealt with the standard customary topics for such a family-type daily, so politics was one of the major topics, given the circumstances in the country in which the -- this paper was issued, but it also dealt with other customary topics which are usually dealt with by other papers; sports, culture, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And there may be a small mistake in the transcript, but just to be clear, you only started work with Glas Javnosti in 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then from 2004 you took up your present position that you now hold as chief of marketing in an IT company?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were working with Intervju magazine back in 1991, on the 24th of November, 1991, did you decide to go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The fighting around Vukovar had ceased then, and we, the editorial office, decided to try and obtain interviews from some persons we assessed to have had a significant role in what had transpired in Vukovar. Primarily we wanted to speak to Major Sljivancanin, given the fact that several days before that he had been shown on all -- in many -- in -- news programmes on television, in a conversation, or rather having a an argument with a Red Cross representative, and this particular footage made Major Sljivancanin -- TV footage made Major Sljivancanin absolutely the best-known officer of the then Yugoslav People's Army, so that we decided to make an interview with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Before you arrived in Vukovar on that day, had you organised, had you made arrangements with Major Sljivancanin for that interview?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: No. We had not. We had no way of contacting him and making any arrangements. The only thing that we could arrange was to establish contact through our journalists who had been to Vukovar before that and had already written for our paper, so to organise -- to have him organise for somebody to take us through Vukovar and establish contact with Major Sljivancanin and try to be granted that interview from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How did you get to Vukovar, and who travelled with you in your group?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: We travelled in a car of one of our associates, and that is a journalist who have been to Vukovar before. There were four of us; three of us journalists, and one photo reporter -- reporter/photographer. At the entrance to Vukovar, we came met with -- we came across one of the volunteers who had spent a long time there, and the agreement was that he would meet us there and take us into Vukovar as we supposed, on the basis of the information that we have gathered before that, that it would indeed be difficult to get into the city because of all the devastation in the streets and because the army would not allow civilians, including journalists, to walk around the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. About how long did you spend in Vukovar on that day, the 24th of November?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime from the morning hours, when we got there, until 4.00 or 5.00 p.m., not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during that day, is it fair to say whilst you were at Vukovar, that you didn't get to speak to Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is right. We did not get to speak to him that day. We did not get to speak to him in Vukovar, better to put it, but only that evening in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you conducted an interview with him that evening in Belgrade that was published in the Intervju magazine a few days later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were in Vukovar on that day, you interviewed one other person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that day I conducted an interview with Captain Radic in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it also correct that that interview was published in Intervju magazine, the same issue as which Mr. Sljivancanin's interview was published a few days later?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. It was published -- this interview was also published in the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I will ask you a few questions in detail about how both interviews were conducted. But before we do that, perhaps if you could describe to the Court what you did when you got to Vukovar that day, from the time that you arrived to the time that you left. Just to put these interviews in some sort of context. And take your time.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: We arrived in Vukovar in the morning. At the approach to the city, the entrance to Vukovar, we met this -- we were met by this volunteer who took over as a driver of our car, and then he took some roads that he knew and took us through to the centre of Vukovar. We then asked him to take us to the very centre of Vukovar, because it seemed to us that the most interesting area would be around the Vukovar Hospital, which was already known on the basis of previous TV reports, so we wanted to be there, in the vicinity of that hospital. He drove us up to very near, a spot very near the hospital. We dared not approach to the hospital, the hospital itself, because he thought that there were troops there that would prevent us from taking a tour of the hospital and that it would not be good for us to be seen by them, that we should rather get out of the car and inspect the surroundings. So we were there, near the hospital, we parked our car. And the moment we had just gotten out of the car, a group of officers came in a car, in their car, and they pulled up and stopped by our car -- by us. They were very surprised to see that we should be there as journalists, as civilians, and they asked us to make ourselves scarce immediately, and explained to us that, inter alia, that it was dangerous for us to be there because the terrain was still being cleared up. There were still some mines there, and they didn't want to assume any responsibility for anything that might happen to us. Nevertheless, we managed to make a -- to agree with -- to stay there for a while, promising that we would not go far from the place where they had found us, that later we would be leaving Vukovar, so that we had occasion to spend some time in that street near the hospital. And across from that point we could see a terrifying scene. There was a yard, and some people in uniform who worked there told us -- who worked removing corpses told us that that was the infirmary of the -- or the dispensary of the hospital, and that in the yard of that infirmary there were several tens of corpses, bodies. We recorded that, we actually photographed that, and published in the same issue of the magazine Intervju, where the talks, the interviews with these officers were published. After a short tour of sight-seeing, so to speak, we went away from there, following -- on the proposal of Radak, I believe, who was our guide through Vukovar, and we went up to a house on a hill, a bit farther from the centre of Vukovar, and as they told us that was some sort of a headquarters of the Territorial Defence, Territorial Defence staff, or the house of the commanders of the Territorial Defence. That house was half demolished, but there several people inside. We were introduced to them, we said what our objective was, why we had come, and we asked them to help us get in touch with representatives of the army, so that we could get hold of Major Sljivancanin. But they were unable to arrange that for us, but they told us that perhaps it would be good for us to talk to Captain Radic, who was also a JNA officer, and who they expected would be arriving at that house shortly, at a certain point in time, but they were not actually sure that he would come, and they were not sure of the time when he would come. So I decided to wait there to see whether this captain would indeed show up and to try and obtain an interview from him. After a while Captain Radic indeed appeared. I introduced myself and proposed to him that we talk about or, rather, that I interview him about what had happened in Vukovar and what his impressions were. Initially he refused, but later on he did agree to it, so that we sat in the kitchen of that house and had this talk, the content of which was published in the next issue of Intervju. My colleagues and some other people who were there around us told me, after I had finished the talk with Radic, that they had somehow managed to get in touch with representatives of the army and that they were given a promise that we could try and obtain an interview from Major Sljivancanin, but not there, not in Vukovar, but perhaps in Belgrade once the army had gone from -- had withdrawn from Vukovar, and that had been planned for exactly that day and was actually in course in Vukovar. Then we set out for Belgrade and arrived there in the evening. In the evening, we rang the phone numbers that we were given -- had been given and established -- got in touch with Mr. -- Major Sljivancanin, and he received us sometime around 10.00 p.m. And we met in the premises of the Guards Brigade and had this talk or were given this interview that we published a few days later in the next issue of Intervju.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Just to perhaps clear up one matter: In the statement that you gave to the OTP, an investigator from the Tribunal back in 2003, it states that you saw Major Sljivancanin in -- in Vukovar. Is that correct or not? From what you've said, you didn't see him there but saw him later.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I met Major Sljivancanin, saw him in the flesh, only in the evening of the 24th, when we had the interview granted in Belgrade. Before that I had had no occasion to ever meet him. I only saw him in TV programmes in this famous footage which all TVs were playing in the days before, with Major Sljivancanin prominently featuring, and it impressed me, so I remember that. But I did not meet him in the flesh before the 24th of November in the evening in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just very briefly, can you tell the Court the context in which you saw Major Sljivancanin in that film clip that you saw before you went to Vukovar? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: It was a clip which was a photograph in front of the hospital or thereabouts, Major Sljivancanin was talking to the representative of the Red Cross or -- and explaining to him that he was the man in charge, that Major Sljivancanin was the man in charge there, that people from the Red Cross, from international organisations, could not come there and tell them what to do or how things were to be done. And that was more or less the content or the context of that programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps if we just go back to now to some particular details of your day in Vukovar, I would just like it talk about the driver, the guide that took you around Vukovar and then took you to the Territorial Defence headquarters. You said his name was Radak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Sasa Radak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he tell you his nickname?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. His nickname was either Cetinje, or Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe him. Was he a civilian, a military person, can you describe what group he may have belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection now, he looked like someone who was not a member of the regular army. He wore a beard and looked unkempt for a regular army member. And I believe that he himself actually told me that he was a volunteer in Vukovar, and that he had found himself in Vukovar precisely in that capacity, having come there as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he tell you if he belonged to a specific unit or not? And, if he did, which unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: He did not say anything directly to me. I did not talk much to him. In the text which was published in the same issue of the Intervju, which was made by a colleague who was there with me, Radak stated that he was a member of a unit that they called the death squad, or the death platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you got to the headquarters of the Territorial Defence, you said there were some people inside. Can you describe those people; were they civilians or did they have something to do with -- with the military?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, all of them were civilians. More or less they had some pieces of military clothing on them. I suppose that they were perhaps members of the Vukovar Territorial Defence, but definitely they were not regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long were you at the -- these headquarters before Captain Radic came?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I suppose about one hour, not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And before he came, did any of the Territorial Defence members, or people that you believed may have been part of the Territorial Defence, did they talk about him? Did they talk about Captain Radic? And if they did, what did they say?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember now what they said. I know that based on what we heard we gained an impression that Captain Radic was a well-respected army officer and that he was the person that we should interview and that we should make public what he had to say, what his experiences were. This is one of the main reasons why we decided to interview him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when he arrived at the headquarters, what happened before the interview started?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He greeted some of the people who were there. Since the army was leaving on that day, as far as I could gather, he came precisely to say good-bye to those members of the TO. Once they said their good-byes, I introduced myself and suggested that we interview him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you introduced yourself, I assume you stated your name and the magazine that you worked for?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think your testimony has been that he was initially reluctant to participate in the interview, but finally agreed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Initially he refused it, but after I insisted, as did the people who were in the house, somehow we managed to convince him to have a short interview. He excused himself, saying that he had a lot of work, the army had to be evacuated from there, but we promised him that it wouldn't take too long, and then we finally interviewed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You may have said it already, but where in the house did you interview Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that was in some kind of a kitchen that was in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was present at the interview, other than yourself and Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: We were mostly alone. I think that occasionally somebody would come in, pass through the kitchen, but it would -- it was mostly just the two of us, and this is how we managed to complete it rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just going to ask you a few questions now about how the interview was recorded and then we'll talk about the substance of some of it. When you interviewed him, did you take notes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How did you take the notes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I put questions and wrote down answers in my notebook by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When did you type up those notes, or did someone type them up for you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we did that on the following day. I retyped them myself, because those were my notes, and I can decipher them best. So I did that on the following day, on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then the interview was published in the magazine sometime later that week; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was the interview that was published accurate to the answers that Captain Radic gave you when you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. I tried to convey the conversation that we had as accurately as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would now like to give you a copy of the interview that was published in the magazine with the usher's assistance. Thank you. This is Rule 65 ter number 36, and the B/C/S version of the magazine interview is 0119-2172 to 73. And the English version is 0059-3913 to 15. Now, if I can ask that we call up the English version on Sanction, which we have here. I would now like to ask you a couple of questions. Is the document in front of you the interview that was published with Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In that interview you asked Captain Radic the question: "What was the fighting that you took part in like?" And he mentioned a little further down: "I lost three tanks the first day. One of them was burnt completely, and the other two were damaged, but not beyond repair." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see a burnt tank near the Territorial Defence headquarters when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In a street in the vicinity of that house we saw a tank, a disabled tank, and somebody told us that that was one of the tanks which had been put out of action there in the course of the combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, of course I'm not going ask you to read out the whole interview, because we have it here. But I would just like to focus on a couple of points. You asked Captain Radic: "Who were your soldiers?" And then he responded, the people that he commanded. I was wondering whether you could read that passage out to the Court. Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: "When asked 'who were your soldiers,' he replied, 'at one point in time, in the company which I commanded there were about 500 people of different ethnicity and different party affiliations. There were active servicemen, volunteers, reservists, Chetniks and Serbian volunteers among them. I had to unite them all under one command to ensure success. That was achieved with hard work at all times of day and night. It sometimes happened that commanders would come to fetch me at 1.00 or 2.00 p.m. [as interpreted] and ask for help. If a senior officer refuses to help people under such circumstances, he loses his authority. I felt responsible, and I had to do it, both for their sakes and my own.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you also asked him, if we look at the interview, the following question: "When you analysed the course of the battle for Vukovar, it seems as though the confrontation line did not move for weeks. What exactly happened when Vukovar fell?" And then he answered that question in a number of different ways. But about halfway down that paragraph, he starts to talk about how he commanded, how he exercised command over the different groups under him. I've highlighted a passage in your original there. Could you read out the passage that was in response to that particular question?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: "It was then that I made it perfectly clear to all soldiers, reservists, volunteers, active servicemen or Vukovar TO members, how they could fight and who could do that. Active servicemen and reservists who had come with me from Belgrade had to stay and fight because of circumstances beyond their control. I did not give the TO members the opportunity to decide whether they wanted to fight or not. It was their town and they had to fight for it. The volunteers who had come from Serbia and Montenegro and other parts belonged to different groups. Some were adventurers who had come to experience the turmoil of war, some were looters and robbers. Some simply tried to be patriots, realised it wasn't for them and wanted to return home. That's why I gave the volunteers a choice. The first one was to obey my every order and work according to my plan; or, second, to go home without any further explanation."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And then if we go further down the interview, in finishing up the interview, you asked him the question: "Today, as you leave Vukovar, what is the most important lesson you have learned during the fighting?" Can you just read the first two paragraphs of that answer, and then the rest we will tender to the Court later.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: "Those who do not understand what a war is should come to Vukovar and see how much sweat, pain and effort invested during the last 50 years can be destroyed in just two months. Vukovar became a ghost town in just two months. Previously I never had occasion to see a dead man, and here in Vukovar I turned to stone in two months. For me, now, to see in one place, 100, 200 or 500 dead, or just one dead person, and then ... I mean, those who have survived the war in Vukovar cannot leave this place with a clear conscience and the frame of mind they had before. People bear deep psychological traumas, and this will certainly haunt them for a very long time. I used to shy away from seeing a slaughtered animal before, and now I've grown used to it all."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. We've finished with discussing some aspects of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender the interview. It's the ERN numbers I have read oath, the B/C/S and the English. And it's under 65 ter number 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 353.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, about how long did the interview take?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: About half an hour. I don't remember exactly, but half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After the interview was finished, how long did you stay at the headquarters before leaving?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we didn't stay long following that. We got ready to travel back, and then shortly thereafter we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was Captain Radic still there when you left, or had he left earlier?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think that he had left earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In the Intervju magazine another article appears in addition to the interview with Sljivancanin, Captain Radic and Sasa Radak, there was an article about Spasoje Petkovic, a soldier in Vukovar. Did you meet him that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't meet with him, but as far as I remember, one of my colleagues who were there with me talked to him approximately at the same time when I talked to Captain Radic. I'm not sure whether the conversation took place in front of the house, outside of the house, where Radic and I were, or somewhere in the vicinity. But at any rate, it took place simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see Petkovic that day, or is it just the information you received from your colleague that you understood that he was there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether -- whether I saw him that day or later. He came to our office once he was no longer a soldier. I think I saw him back in Vukovar, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In any event, you received information from your colleague that he interviewed Petkovic at that same headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct. At the time while I talked to Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although I am a bit late with my remark, the witness didn't say that the talk took place in the headquarters. He said somewhere in the vicinity, and in the vicinity is not the same as headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's technically correct. He did earlier say that whether it was inside, outside, or in the vicinity, but my friend is correct. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, when you went back to Belgrade, you said that you interviewed Major Sljivancanin. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That evening, upon our return to Belgrade from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where did you interview him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: At the headquarters of the Guards Brigade. In one of the offices there. I suppose that that was Major Sljivancanin's office. Or an office of one of his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you record the interview in the same way that you recorded the interview with Captain Radic, or did you do it differently this time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I certainly did note it down. I wrote it by hand in my notebook. And I think that we also taped it on a tape recorder, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "we," was anyone else present interviewing, in addition to yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a colleague of mine there, and also a photographer. There were a total of three of us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the notes of that interview, when were they typed up?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: On the following day, Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the interview that appeared in the Intervju magazine on the 29th of November, 1991, is that an accurate record of the answers that Mr. Sljivancanin gave you to your questions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I hope so. We always tried to convey statements and interviews correctly. I think that this is an accurate reflection of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it correct that you met Major Sljivancanin on a number of occasions after this interview over the last 15 years or so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many times did you meet him, and in what context were those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 10 times under various circumstances. Sometimes we sought help. We as editors, needed certain information. So we sought help from Major Sljivancanin. One of the most interesting issues in which he helped us was that after a year or so he enabled us to visit the White Palace, which was presidential residence, and it was closed to the public. Due to Major Sljivancanin's intervention, we were able to get inside the building, tour it, and photograph it, and publish it. And then on some occasions we would meet informally and greet each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the relationship you established during that interview with Major Sljivancanin led to a good cooperation between the two of you to enable these -- this type of contact to occur later?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps now if we can look just briefly at the substance of some of the answers given by Major Sljivancanin. Again, we won't read out the interview, it's there to be read by others, but I'd like to concentrate on a couple of parts. And I'm referring to, for the record, 65 ter number 36, and the English version is 0059-3890 to 95. And then B/C/S version is 0119-2169 to, last two digits again, 71. Witness, if you look at tab 2, you will see the interview that you had with -- the record of the interview with Major Sljivancanin. And I've been advised that the English version of the interview is in Sanction, and the witness has the B/C/S version in front of him. Witness, do you have a copy of the interview in your language in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if we go to the first question after your introductory remarks in the interview. You state: "You say that in the course of fighting in Vukovar the last days were the most difficult for you. Why?" Do you see that question?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can just take your time and read the highlighted text that follows immediately after that question.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: "First I have to say one thing. There were great heroes among soldiers in Vukovar. These were young kids, younger than 18, whom I admired. I am proudly stating that it was very good that there were Macedonian, Muslims and Croats among them, people of all nationalities. This war was a completely new experience, both for myself and my soldiers. While we waged the war, in the evening we would plan what was to be done at night and what tasks were to be completed on the following day. "At night, after completing my work at the command and issuing assignments, I would drive around with a driver. Initially it was the late Slobodan Popovic, and later Rajko Tomic. We had a map of Vukovar and knew exactly who was in which house at any given moment. We would pass through one field to the next and spend most of the time where the main combat took place. We even went to see our artillery observation post officers who helped us adjust the distance to the target during the shelling. "During the day we killed all the Ustashas who had crossed our path. You see, we had no other choice, they fired at us, and we fired at them. And may the best man win. That was war, after all."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can look at a particular answer that appears further down the interview, when you ask him the question: "What exactly did the ICRC representative want from you?" Now you had previously spoken about, I think, the video clip that you saw before you went to Vukovar and asked some questions about that. But particularly, what did he say in response to that question: "What exactly did the ICRC representative want from you?"

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the question aimed at clarifying how that infamous footage came to be filmed and this was his response. He complained about having to wait very long. Well, I had to wait very long, too, and I also had to lead the fighting. So if we had to wait then you have to wait too, until the following day, if necessary. It was probably all pre-staged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's the -- the last part of that -- the last part of the paragraph. And I think we can leave the previous bit for the moment. And I would like to ask you one last question about this particular interview. In the following question after that answer you asked: "Did you know about a secret agreement between the Croatian authorities and the International Red Cross?" And he explains, he gives an answer to that. But I've highlighted a portion that is at the end of that answer, and if you could read that answer out to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: "Regardless of all of their discussions, I did my job, just like my soldiers and officers did. We tried to assist every citizen in danger and carry out all of our tasks with precision, although we had lost many soldiers, officers and volunteers, none of the soldiers of the territorial forces under my command tried to take revenge when Ustashas surrendered to us. They behaved with great dignity, heroism and chivalry. That was a major thing. When my sergeant, Popovic, or perhaps it should be soldier Popovic was killed, I also felt as though I should kill a thousand Ustashas to avenge the death of that young person. He was killed and was not at fault, because as a corporal of this country he was unable to move freely through it and was fired upon. Nevertheless, when I saw all those prisoners later, I never -- it never even occurred to me that all of them should be killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. After -- after that interview was completed and in the following occasions where you met Sljivancanin because of that relationship that developed, did he ever complain about the interview that was published being inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after you had the interview with Captain Radic, did you ever see or speak to him again?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: No, no. We didn't see each other ever again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like you to say -- explain -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just being reminded, Your Honour, by the case manager that I should not forget to tender that document. I've indicated the ERN numbers, and it was from 65 ter 36, and I would seek to tender that interview with Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received. Oh, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no objection to this document being tendered as evidence, but I should like to ask you one thing. I have checked the English translation, or parts of this text, not the entire text, and parts -- those parts which were important for me were okay. But now, specifically speaking, when we are reading one part of this transcript, I believe that the English part does not in some parts correspond to the actual text when the -- specifically when the witness was reading the first part of the interview, the B/C/S version said: "Well, come what may or whatever, end of the sticker, whoever gets, it is war," in the English, the official translation is: "May the best man win." Perhaps it seems to you that these things are too minor, but I would like to ask verification of this translation for tomorrow. I should just like to place this on record if there are no great discrepancies between these two meanings in the English translation, then I shall be satisfied. But we -- by the way, we only got the English translation this morning. That is why I have only made this comparison now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's what the English call colloquial language, but certainly I'll ask the court officer to try to arrange for just verification of the interpretation of that passage for you, Mr. Lukic. The document is received.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 354, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just for the record, an unrevised translation had been provided to the Defence a long time ago. And the -- this particular English translation was provided yesterday. It -- because it appeared more revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if we can go back now to when you arrived in Vukovar. You said that you went to some sort of clinic or some place where you saw a number of bodies, and that place was near the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe that place in relation to where it was from the hospital, how far away was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: It was several hundred metres away from the hospital. It was, as they told us at the time, some sort of an infirmary, and in the court of this -- in the yard of this infirmary there were bodies. Those that were there, that we found there, the people namely, they all thought that these were bodies of Serbian civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Some of the soldiers or some of the men in uniform who were working to pull out the bodies from that yard, and the pulling out of the bodies from the yard was in course precisely [as interpreted] as we arrived on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll just now show you a video clip in Sanction. It's from Exhibit 136. The timer is two minutes 58 to three minutes and 25, and it's from a larger clip of six minutes and 15 seconds. And I would like you to have a look amount the clip to see whether you recognise -- recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
