utterances.text: Witness, looking at that clip, are you able to say whether that was the same place that you went to when you arrived at Vukovar that you just talked about, or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: It seems to be that place. It resembles very much the place that I was at, and the photographs that we published from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that exhibit has been tendered, so there is no need for me to tender it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: 136, Your Honour. Two minutes 58 to three minutes and 25 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, can you -- firstly, did you go to the centre of town when you were being shown around by Radak, Sasa Radak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were more or less near the centre of town. We passed by some roads and came near the hospital. Then we walked for several hundred metres around there to where the -- as long as it was safe, in our assessment. There were some soldiers there, and we didn't want to draw their attention. And these were the scenes that we saw there in Vukovar, and then we went back to the hotel on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What are some of the buildings that you remember in the centre of town when you walked there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: The hotel is actually a house, a building that I remember most vividly, and of course I remember the other ruins. I remember the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After leaving Vukovar on the 24th of November, did you ever return to Vukovar? And, if you did, on about how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was there later on a couple of occasions, two or three times in the following two or three years --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But the interpreter is not sure she heard the last part of the sentence correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It's not completely clear from the transcript, Witness, about how many times you went back to Vukovar. First, how many times did you go back?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: So after that, after this visit in 1991, I went to Vukovar two or three times in the following two or three years, until 1994 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the purpose for you to go back there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I took delegations of foreign journalists there, as well as the representatives of different foreign political institutions in order to show them what the result or war looked like. And then they themselves wanted to see Vukovar, which had, by that time, become the symbol of the conflict in our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you went back on those occasions, would you take them to the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe the destruction you saw in Vukovar when you went there on the 24th of November, particularly in the town centre and generally in other places?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: What I remember is that we didn't see a single whole house that had not been destroyed. The entire city was devastated and was very -- the whole city were impassable some of the streets were virtually impassable, so that we could hardly pass by car to reach the hospital. I really don't know what else I could say. The whole city was a shambles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In a minute -- in a moment we'll just show you a video clip to see if you can recognise anything within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But shortly after that, I think because e-court takes a little time to pull up a map, I would ask that through e-court the Vukovar town map, 0468-7703, if that could be called up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit 156 probably will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you're not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean you want the high-density one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Neither. Your Honour, we're upgrading the map. We haven't had a map in this case, unfortunately, with the street names as specific as we would like and the street names that applied back in 1991. This is a new map that we think will help connect some evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. I was trying to help the registry. I will be quiet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It's greatly appreciated in any event, Your Honour. If we can show the video now, please. And it's 65 ter number 310, at one hour 28 minutes and 39 seconds to one hour 29 minutes and 50 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, were you able to see that video clip on your screen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you recognise what the video was of?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are recognisable buildings from Vukovar. That is the environment of the hotel, the surroundings of the hotel, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And which hotel are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: This is a hotel in Vukovar on the river-bank, which is a symbol of the devastated city. I believe that its name was the Dunav Hotel, the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were there any differences in the video clip you saw to what you saw when you arrived on the 24th of November and looked around the city centre, in terms of the damage?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are no substantial differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender that video. We received it from an organisation called Filmske Novosti, it's a film archive company in Serbia and Montenegro, and they provided that footage to us in 2000. And the footage has been recorded as coming from a time period after the fall of Vukovar. It may be after, it may be shortly before, from the shooting, I'm not sure, but we would be seeking to tender that video clip. And the ERN number is V000-0625.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 355.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I can call the Vukovar town map, the new map with the street names, 0468-7703.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the map in front of you on your screen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if I could ask the registry assistant to enlarge, say, the centre of Vukovar up a little further. Thank you. Witness, on that map do you see the location of where the hospital is? There is a legend on the left-hand side, but I believe you've seen that legend before. Do you see where the hospital is on that map?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to mark that location, say, with a large letter A, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me just see how.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Territorial Defence headquarters, which you interviewed Captain Radic in, can you put the approximate location of where that was, if you are able?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I could only do that approximately. I suppose it was in this section which is called Petrova Gora, and I believe that that is somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why do you think that the headquarters were in Petrova Gora, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Because in one of the texts which we published in that issue from my colleague who talked to a soldier, I believe Petkovic, said that he had found him in the settlement of Petrova Gora, and I suppose that that is where I had been, and where I had talked to Captain Radic. I remember that we had to climb uphill from the hospital up to this house where we interviewed Radic, and that is all as far as my recollection and knowledge of this particular topic goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this annotated map, and also a blank version of the map as well. And also I believe we have a -- an English version of the legend of that map as well. So those three -- three exhibits. And I believe that the procedure is that the English version and the B/C/S version, which really relates to the legend, normally gets one exhibit number. I'm in Your Honour's hands on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The map that has been marked will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 356, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The map itself will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 357, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the legends will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may have confused the issue. We have a map an English legend on it. So that we have two versions of the same map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The legend will be received, the English legend will be received as part of Exhibit 357.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And, just for the record, Your Honour, this map was obtained from the Vukovar museum. We received it earlier this month; obviously the Defence have a copy. And it's a street map of Vukovar which was dated in 1984. And the street names would have been the names that applied in 1991. If Your Honour just bears with me for 30 seconds, I'm just finalising.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you may have mentioned this already, but you did your national service in Croatia in 1982 for 12 months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Obviously with the time we must take the second break now. And we will resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kacarevic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me introduce myself. I am Vladimir Domazet, one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Mrksic. I will be putting questions to you on behalf of the defence of Mr. Mrksic. Right at the outset let me please ask you to bear in mind that we speak the same language and that there is a need to make a pause between question and answer, so that the interpreters can do their job. Mr. Kacarevic, when answering in examination-in-chief, you gave us some information about your biography and career, and it seems that you spent the majority of your career as a journalist, but you are not working as one now; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How long has it been since you stopped working as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Approximately two years, from the beginning of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you were employed in the marketing department of a company. Unless it's a problem for you, would you tell us what company you work for?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Is that necessary? I work for a company called Informatika A.D., from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Kacarevic, if I understood it correctly, it seems that you graduated when you were 28 or 29, but you had worked as a journalist prior to that, first of all, for a paper called Student?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First for Student, and then for Politika.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When answering my learned friend's questions you spoke about Student and how influential it was at a certain point in time. Let me ask you this: I can't remember exactly, although I did follow that paper for a long time, did you work there during the period of time when it was frequently banned from working by court injunction, due to its political writings and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there at the time when that paper had a lot of typical problems with the authorities. When I was there, there were no injunctions banning our work during that one year; however, there were changes in the leadership, among the editors of the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And when you moved from Student to Politika, that was an advancement in your career. You said that Politika was an influential paper, and the same goes for the publishing company. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You described Politika as a prominent, influential daily; I will fully agree with you. Especially given that it is one of the oldest dailies, not only in Serbia, but perhaps in Europe as well. During the period of time when you worked there, was there a time when, in view of many in Serbia, Politika did not live up to its former glory, to its former reputation, especially when it came to political articles and those dealing with internal politics?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: It depends on how you judge it. The period of time when I came to Politika was not known as one of its golden days, hey days, but later on it resumed its former influence. It depends on what the relations are between the politicians and the paper. Sometimes one side is stronger and sometimes the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that period of time was not the most glorious one for Politika. I think that that was the time when that there was that infamous show-down between the late Milosevic and late Stambolic and that the paper Politika was used as a means to fight each other.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I came to Politika immediately after the death of Josip Broz Tito, and during that period of time the role of Politika was a much simpler one. There were no particular diverse currents in the political life of Serbia. Later on, after 1984 and 1985, certain factions became to emerge, but soon thereafter I left Politika myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely the period I was referring to, 1988 and 1989, when you left Politika. That was the period that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you moved to the paper called Intervju in 1991, you described the kind of work that you did when you went to Vukovar, and at that time you worked as a journalist in Intervju; is that right? You did not hold a higher position?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I did prior to that. Several months upon starting to work for Intervju I worked as assistant editor, and then I moved to a position just below that, and then after that I was a journalist and a member of the editorial board at the time when these interviews in Vukovar when made.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: While you were at Intervju, did you have any problems with -- with anything? Did you leave that paper because of the problems you encountered, or what was the reason when you moved to Glas Javnosti -- or no, you went to the printing to the press first. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, initially there were no problems when I started working in Intervju, and later on the leadership was removed, so all of us had to step down, take a position a step below. That was a period of time when it became increasingly difficult to work at Intervju, and it ended with my resignation. That's when I moved to a different job.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Am I to understand that the reasons were of political nature? Was some political pressure exerted, or were they dissatisfied with your work, that of yours and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: The reasons were mostly of political nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: While you worked for the printing press, you certainly weren't employed there as a journalist, so I'm not going to ask you about this. But you said that starting in 1989 you began to work for Glas Javnosti. I can't recall now precisely, but I think that that paper was created once a conflict broke down in a paper called Blic, and so -- that was another renowned daily, and after some journalists split from that paper, Glas Javnosti was created. Was that when you started working for them or a bit later?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: A bit later, the following year. Glas Javnosti was established in 1988 and I started working for them in nineteen-eighty --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 1998, and I started working for them 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: In January. I was director from January to July, and then in August I became editor-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When speaking of the period of time when you worked for Intervju and the problems you had which led to your departure, was -- were the reasons for your leaving Glas Javnosti similar? Did you have those problems or other ones?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I had problems, but of different nature. Not the same ones as when I worked for Intervju.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm now going to turn to a different topic; namely, your trip to Vukovar on the 24th of November. I think you said that there were a total of four of you travelling there; three journalists and a photographer, photo journalist. Who were your colleagues who travelled with you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Vlahovic, Bosko Sajkovic, and Slavenko Bojovic, he was the photographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So the photographs of Vukovar were made by the photographer you mentioned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. We also had an amateur camera with us. The photographer used his equipment, whereas the three of us shared that camera among us, and we made pictures that seemed important to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now that we're dealing with this topic, let me ask you this: You have in front of you the paper which published the interviews, and interview with soldier Petkovic is among them. We can see his photograph there, and it is indicated that Zeljko Sinobad was the photographer who took that picture. Can you explain his involvement? How come his photograph was included if he was not travelling with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I can only guess how this came about. Zeljko Sinobad, as far as I know, worked for Ilustrovana Politika which was in the same building as Intervju. I think that we borrowed that photograph from Zeljko. Incidentally, Zeljko had spent a lot of time in Vukovar himself. He most likely had a photograph with Petkovic, and our paper borrowed the photograph from him. We indicated authorship, even though the photograph was not made by our staff member.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You also spoke of some problems that you had in the centre of Vukovar once they realised that you were a crew of journalists. My question is: How did you reach Vukovar? Did you encounter any problems, were there any check-points, did you need any kind of passes? We have some witnesses who described that period of time to us, so I'm interested in how you travelled from Belgrade to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one needed passes. We had one such pass. And we had to produce it at the check-point near Sid. Later on we thought that those passes would not be valid anymore, at least that's what we were told, so we tried to find a local person, somebody with local contacts who would us get through, so that we wouldn't be stopped at another check-point. This is why a colleague of mine got in touch with Sasa Radak who then escorted us through Vukovar to the place where we wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, the only point where you had to produce those passes was near Sid, and later on you had no other problems in reaching Vukovar. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember who gave you that pass? I'm not interested in how you procured that pass but, rather, in who issued such passes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: As to who issued the pass for us on that occasion, I'm not sure. I think it was some kind of a military service, but I don't know where it was located or how one went about procuring one. I think that the secretary of our paper obtained it for us, but I don't remember because we personally did not participate in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The person that you mentioned, Sasa Radak, who was your contact, who was supposed to facilitate your stay in Vukovar, did he wait for you outside of Vukovar, or in Vukovar town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was on the approach of Vukovar, outside of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But prior to that, or after meeting up with him, nobody stopped you again except for that group of officers, JNA officers, whom you met in the centre of the town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that one of your colleagues got in touch with Sasa Radak. Do you know additional details about that? How did they meet, did they know each other personally, or was there a mediator who introduced them to each other?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure how exactly we got in touch with Radak. I knew -- I know that this was the information we had from Belgrade. Prior to setting out we knew that a local person who was well familiar with the terrain would be awaiting us there. However, I wasn't the one establishing this contact, so I don't know how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Apart from this issue of the 29th of November when all these interviews and articles were published, did you personally, or your paper, write about Vukovar at all prior to that date?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The paper did publish accounts from the battlefield in Vukovar, but I personally wrote nothing on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember and can you say something about the general atmosphere that prevailed there prior to the fall of Vukovar in the months running up to the fall of the city? Was there anything like a media campaign, you know what that is, where there are stories of Vukovar, about the atrocities there, from the Croatian side, and how was this covered in the media, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: The atmosphere was one of -- such that one could experience the conflict in Vukovar as a sort of a civil war, and it was expected for the regular army, the troops of the JNA, to actually resolve that conflict. When the fighting for Vukovar -- the battles for Vukovar ended, in the public looked like the arrival of the American cavalry in western movies. That is why some of the people, some of the officers from the army, like Major Sljivancanin, who appeared on television precisely in those days was so -- was so popular. He appeared in a very short clip. And because before that the JNA had in no way been personified in the media. They did talk about the Vukovar and the conflict in Vukovar, but the public was not able to be acquainted with any particular officer or person featuring there. It was all only very terse statements on the role of the army. That was the first appearance of Major Sljivancanin, when the public could see an officer talking to you, addressing you, someone who was the personification of the people's army. Most of the public saw this at that time -- for most of the public this was a relief. It was an end of a terrible conflict on which horrible accounts had reached the public in terms of what was happening inside Vukovar, which was controlled by armed groups, who did this on behalf of the Croatian state, the nascent Croatian state, so it seemed that the JNA was coming there to put an end to all that chaos, to all that uncontrolled conflict and blood shed. And that was more or less the context at the end of the battle for Vukovar, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Precisely what you said just a while ago; namely, that I suppose there were in the public and the -- also there were there stories in the public that also reached you as journalists, were stories launched by the other side on all the abominations and atrocities in Vukovar? Can you explain to us in more detail what was being published in those days in the media in that respect?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the details. I can just talk about my impressions from that period. There was a widespread conviction in the public which was also pushed through the media, through rumours, and in different other ways, seeing that Vukovar is quite near Belgrade and that there was a circulation of people, there were refugees who were coming from there. So there was an atmosphere in which people believed that in Vukovar, which was controlled by the armed forces of the Croatian side, there were being committed horrendous crimes against the Serb civilians there, that there existed a different private prisons in cellars and basements of houses and other private places, that it was necessary as soon as possible to deliver those people there from such terror, and that was the widespread conviction. It was the prevalent conviction at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you speak about this, are you referring to things that were heard and published in the media or both? Namely, was this something that one could hear in Belgrade where you were also, from other sources, not only from the media and from the media?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to give you a precise answer to that particular question. This was the public impression. Now how much of it was from media sources and how much was from rumours, I really can't say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: To wrap up this subject, at least as far as I'm concerned, my colleagues might have more questions, to the best of your recollection as a journalist, as a contemporary of the events, it was thus expected that the disarming of the people involved would actually lead to some sort of a peace in Vukovar, and this is what was expected in Belgrade and people actually rejoiced in Belgrade when that indeed happened?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember sometime around that year, in view of the events that were transpiring in Croatia, do you remember the affairs or the scandals known in the public and not only in the public as opera, opera and Labrador, or more specifically, more concretely speaking --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: More specifically, it was the arrest of a large group in Croatia accused of being the collaborators of civilian and military counter-intelligence services for the account of the JNA, i.e., Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As a journalist, did you write anything about it, or did you have any information about what that was particular -- specifically about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not write about it. I tried to find out more at that time, but I was not really successful. I really did not give a very good account of myself in trying to find out what it was about. It was a very interesting topic, and the media cover it widely. There were different versions, but what was the actual truth was not quite certain. It is true that there were arrests, that these secret operations under those designations were indeed referred to and that people were arrested because of that, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But -- and do you remember what happened to that entire group of officers and others who were arrested in Croatia? Were they put on trial eventually in Croatia or did they meet a different fate?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: At this point in time I do not recall with precision, I could not reply to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could jog your memory in some way. Do you remember that there was a significant exchange between Croatia and Serbia, or Croatia and the JNA sometime in the period after the fall of Vukovar? I'm talking about the exchange of people who were in Croatia and those who were imprisoned in Serbia? If you can, if you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that there were such exchanges of prisoners in several instances at that time. I know that there were prisoners from Vukovar, not all of them, but most of them were in the Sremska Mitrovica prison and were from there exchanged for some people from Croatia, so they were let go to Croatia, and I -- that event is etched in my memory, but I cannot recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Of course I understand you cannot remember whether that particular exchange was associated with a group that had been arrested as part of the Labrador affair?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember both as a journalist and someone who was a contemporary of important events, did you write about or did you have any information about Kostic [as interpreted] sometime in September in 1991 -- Gospic, I'm sorry, about Gospic sometime in September in 1991 and important things that were taking place there and could affect the relations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I did not write about that. I know that there was coverage in the media of those developments. The civilians had been killed in Gospic and in the surrounding area in some battles that were fought there, but I cannot remember the details at this point. I know that Gospic was a topic in the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Kacarevic, when you referred to one of these people who feature in your account, that is the soldier Petkovic, I believe that you used the term he used to come many times to our paper, to the editorial office. What were the reasons for his visits to the paper? Was this a person who was desirous of some publicity, or was he after something else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I know for a fact that he came to the editorial office at least once. After that he didn't have much of a contact with me, but I do remember that that time he came to our office because he had left the army, he had taken off his uniform, and he came to say hello -- or actually to say good-bye. What his motives were, I really don't know whether he wanted more publicity, or was he after something else, I really don't know. That I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just revert for a minute to my question regarding Gospic to be more precise. You said what was -- what stories were going on about -- were being bandied about about the killings of civilians, what the nationality, what ethnicity were those civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: They were of Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Gospic itself is a part of Croatia that prior to that war, had been predominantly in a large measure populated by Serbs. Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Gospic there was a Serb population, but whether it was in the minority or in the majority, I don't remember that exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please tell me: In these interviews that came out as regards the titles of these interviews, who actually formulated those titles? Was it you or somebody else in the paper?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: The titles of my own text were mine. And the titles, the captions of other texts were, I suppose, by the editor in charge, and the same goes for the cover page. I -- it is always the duty of the -- or -- of the editor in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to ask you a question given the fact that you have a long journalistic career, and in view of what you yourself have said about some tumultuous periods that we had occasion to witness after Tito's death, after the advent of Milosevic, and after that as well, and the question is: How big was the influence or, rather, was there any pressure on the part of the political leadership while they were in power on the journalistic profession of the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: I shall try to be brief and if it is not enough, please say to. There were pressures, and they were reflected mainly through the election or the appointment of the key people in the different papers and the editorial offices, so the influence of the state or the echelons in power was actually reflected in the appointment of the editorial staff and the management of the papers. And of course there was always some strife there, because the people involved were the -- often argue between themselves for the positions in question, and in between in the interregnum there was some sort of media freedom as far as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it your experience from all these contacts, did the Security Services in that period also have anything to say or influence the appointment of editorial staff, or did they actually infiltrate their own people in papers and editorial offices?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC
utterances.text: The influence of Security Services on different paper management and editorial offices, still today a subject for which proof is very seldom found. It was said at that time as well that such influence indeed did exist, and it was quite blatantly obvious, but there was no evidence to be produced to substantiate such impressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kacarevic. I have no more questions for you. I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if -- it seems to me that perhaps, even though it is not yet the time for our break, that we begin tomorrow, because we do not have a new witness tomorrow, and Mr. Lukic and I will certainly finish tomorrow. So if it pleases the Court, I should like to ask you to start tomorrow. But of course I am prepared and can start now, but that would mean interrupting my questioning at a certain point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, there is no further witness tomorrow; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, Your Honour. I think it was believed that the people that were being recalled were going to be cross-examined at greater length than they were, so maybe a slight miscalculation on our part. We'll have one for Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. I think you should take into consideration in future, the increasing speed with which Defence counsel are getting to the important matters, so we might be able to move more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think in view of that, Mr. Borovic, rather than you spending eight minutes now and then continuing tomorrow, we will adjourn now. Counsel may remember that it was mentioned earlier this week that tomorrow morning new Judges are being sworn in, so we will not be able to commence until, I believe, 9.45. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of April, 2006, at 9.45 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.38 p.m.,
